discussion.intro: Simpli is still new and benefits from broad discussion.
discussion.intro2: The choices we make—spelling, grammar, vocabulary—can be revisited with input from a large community. Below are some topics open for debate.
discussion.discordPlanned: Invite link: see Next steps (maintainers: set PUBLIC_DISCORD_INVITE_URL at build time).
discussion.governanceNote: How to propose changes: discuss publicly (Discord or forum), gather examples, then update the written spec when a decision is made.
discussion.communityBlurb: These topics are open for debate. Share your views and help shape Simpli.
discussion.topicChTitle: Removing « ch » and « c » (using « tj » for /tʃ/)
discussion.topicChDesc: Replacing ch with tj (e.g. child → tjaild, teacher → tiitjer) is a step toward simplicity and consistency—the letter c is one of the most inconsistent in English. It may, however, make Simpli feel less familiar to English speakers and could affect adoption. This is subject to discussion within the community.
discussion.topicVwTitle: V and W: keep both, fuse, or remove W?
discussion.topicVwDesc: Should we keep the sound /w/ (as in who, we, water) distinct from /v/? Fuse v and w into one letter (one sound, one spelling)? Or remove w entirely and use only v? Each choice affects simplicity, the size of the alphabet, and familiarity for English speakers and others.
discussion.topicProperNounsTitle: Proper nouns: keep as is or rewrite?
discussion.topicProperNounsDesc: Names of people, places, and brands: keep the original spelling (e.g. New York, Paris) or rewrite them in Simpli spelling (e.g. Niu York)? Keeping originals is recognizable but breaks the “one sound, one letter” rule; rewriting is consistent but can look unfamiliar. Open for community input.
discussion.topicPlaceNamesTitle: Geographical names: simplified Simpli spelling or each country’s romanization?
discussion.topicPlaceNamesDesc: For cities, countries, regions, and similar names, should we use one simplified Simpli form (consistent with Simpli phonics) or follow each place’s established romanization (official or widely used systems)? Simplified forms are uniform and easier to learn; classical or official spellings match maps, documents, and local usage but mix many conventions. Open for community input.

home.hero: Simpli is a simple international language: English-style words, Indonesian-style grammar, phonetic spelling.
home.concept1: Simpli is a simple international language—a proposed auxiliary language for egalitarian access to communication. It combines minimal grammar with familiar vocabulary so more people can use it quickly.
home.concept2: Whether you already know some English or are looking for a neutral bridge language, Simpli aims to reduce barriers of time, complexity, and geography.

grammarRulesPage.metaDescription: Full list of Simpli grammar rules.
grammarRulesPage.intro: Simpli has about 12 core rules. No conjugation, no gender, no cases.
grammarRulesPage.sectionPronounsBody: Simpli uses one word for all third-person singular: el. There is no separate “it”; el is used for he, she, and it (people and things). So el hav no hard gramer = It has no hard grammar; Yu kan lern el fast = You can learn it fast.
grammarRulesPage.sectionWordOrderBody: Subject – Verb – Object. Examples: mi si yu, wi it bred.
grammarRulesPage.sectionVerbsBody: Verbs never change. Express when with time words: yesterde, now, tumoro. mi go, el go, dey go. Optionally use wil (future) or hav (past or perfect) before the main verb when no time word is given: mi wil go, mi hav finis. When a time word is present, wil and hav are optional and often omitted: tumoro mi go. Use olredi (already done) and stil (still ongoing): mi olredi finis, mi stil wok. hav also means “have” as a main verb (mi hav buk); context distinguishes auxiliary from main verb.
grammarRulesPage.sectionNegationBody: Put no before the verb: mi no go, el no si.
grammarRulesPage.sectionPluralBody: Optional. Use numbers or meni when needed: tu buk, meni haus.
grammarRulesPage.sectionAdjectivesBody: Before the noun, never change form: big haus, red buk.
grammarRulesPage.sectionPossessionBody: Noun + possessor: haus mi = my house, buk yu = your book. You can add of for clarity, but it’s not needed: haus (of) mi, haus (of) broder (of) mi = my brother’s house.
grammarRulesPage.sectionConnectorsBody: and, or, but, becos, so. mi and yu, el no go becos storm.
grammarRulesPage.sectionCompoundsBody: Join words with a hyphen when useful: sun-lait, fast-trein, woter-fud.

grammarPage.numbersBulletBody: Reading numbers aloud can follow East Asian style (34 → tri ten for).

grammarNumbers.intro: For saying numbers aloud, you can use an East Asian–style reading: from large units to small, with tens built as digit + ten + digit (instead of a single word like “thirty-four”).
grammarNumbers.digits: Digits: sero (0), wan … nain (1–9), ten (10). Larger units: hundrad (hundred), tausand (thousand).

essentialWordsPage.elNote: el = he, she, or it (one word for all third-person singular; no separate “it”).

lessonsPage.metaDescription: Starter lessons: greetings, questions, possession, time words, and aspect markers in Simpli.
lessonsPage.title: Starter lessons
lessonsPage.intro: Short modules based on the site grammar and spelling pages. Simpli examples stay in Simpli; this UI is in your language.
lessonsPage.module1Body: Simpli uses Indonesian-style word order (SVO) and no verb conjugation. Time is expressed with words like yesterde, now, tumoro—not by changing the verb. Without a time word, you may add wil (future) or hav (past or perfect); see the Time and aspect lesson.
lessonsPage.module2Body: Possession is noun + possessor: haus mi (my house), buk yu (your book).
lessonsPage.module3Body: Doubled vowels mark length: it vs iit (eat). See the spelling pages for the full chart.
lessonsPage.module4Body: Name the time with words like yesterde or tumoro—the verb stays the same. Without a time word, you may add wil (future) or hav (past or perfect). Use olredi for something already done and stil for something still going on.

samplesPage.whySimpliGloss: Simpli is a simple language. You can learn it fast. It has no hard grammar. Words come from English but the spelling is easy. Every sound has one letter. You read what you see. Many people in the world know some English. For them Simpli is a bridge. They can use it to talk to others. They can use it for work or travel. We want the world to have one simple language. Simpli can be that language.

roots.metaDescription: Simpli roots: real languages and current global usage.
roots.leadP: Simpli is not invented from scratch. It is rooted in real languages and current usage.
roots.grammarP: The grammar is inspired by Indonesian: analytic structure, no verb conjugation, no grammatical gender, optional plurals.
roots.vocabularyP: The vocabulary is based on English—simplified and regularized.
roots.whyP: Familiar vocabulary + minimal grammar = fast learning.
roots.spellingP: Regularized spelling also draws inspiration from Spanish. Spanish typically adapts loanwords to its own sound–letter norms instead of keeping English-style historical spellings—so almost any foreign word can be integrated cleanly. Simpli follows a similar idea. Example: football → futbol—the same kind of adaptation in Spanish and in Simpli.

spelling.metaDescription: Simpli spelling: simplified letters, phonemes, long vowels.

comparison.metaDescription: Simpli vs Indonesian, English, Esperanto, Glosa, Globish.
comparison.intro: Simpli vs Indonesian, English, Esperanto, Glosa, Globish.
comparison.mediumH2: Medium: "Tomorrow, I will see you at my brother's house"
comparison.complexH2: More complex: "Next week I will go to the market to buy food for my family"
comparison.takeawayP: Takeaway: Simpli is simpler than Esperanto, more regular than English, more intuitive than Glosa.
comparison.notEnglishP: Simpli is not “simplified English.” It does not aim to replace English. You can still learn English and enjoy English literature and books while using Simpli as an auxiliary bridge language.

vocabulary.metaDescription: Simpli vocabulary: why English-based, core size, spelling, compounds.
vocabulary.leadP: Simpli vocabulary is based on English, simplified and written phonetically. Below we explain why we chose English rather than another language or invented words, then how the vocabulary works.
vocabulary.whyH2: Why English (and not another language or from scratch)?
vocabulary.whyLeadP: We use English-derived words for practical reasons, not because English is “better” or more neutral. The goal is to lower the barrier to a shared language.
vocabulary.whyBullet1: Already widely learned: More people learn English as a second language than any other. Hundreds of millions already know some English from school, work, or media. Using familiar roots gives them a head start instead of starting from zero.
vocabulary.whyBullet2: International use: English is already used in science, technology, business, and travel. Many terms (computer, hotel, internet, etc.) are already global. Simpli builds on that exposure so new words feel recognizable.
vocabulary.whyBullet3: Why not another language? Spanish, French, Mandarin, or Arabic are also global, but fewer people learn them as a second language worldwide. Choosing one of them would help some learners and leave others with no prior exposure. English, as the most common L2, gives the largest “transfer” benefit.
vocabulary.whyBullet4: Why not from scratch? A fully invented (a priori) vocabulary would be maximally neutral—no nation “owns” it—but it would be much harder to learn. There would be no cognates or familiar roots. Simpli prioritizes quick learnability so that more people can actually use it; English roots are a practical compromise.
vocabulary.whyCloseP: So: we use English as a base for recognition and speed, not as a statement that English is superior. The grammar is simplified and the spelling is regular, so Simpli is still its own system—just one that many can learn faster because the words look and sound familiar.
vocabulary.howBullet1: Core size: About 300–500 essential words for everyday use; the list can be extended as needed.
vocabulary.howBullet2: Spelling: One sound = one letter; long vowels doubled (rad vs rood). See Spelling and Alphabet rationale.

grammarOverview.lead: Simpli uses an analytic grammar inspired by Indonesian.
grammarOverview.bulletPronouns: Pronouns: One word for he, she, and it: el. Simpli does not have a separate “it”; el is used for all third-person singular (people and things). So: el go = he/she/it goes, El hav no hard gramer = It has no hard grammar.
grammarOverview.bulletVerbs: Verbs: Never change form. Time with words (yesterde, now, tumoro). Optionally wil / hav for future or past when no time word; olredi / stil for completed or ongoing.
grammarOverview.bulletPossession: Possession: Noun + possessor: haus mi = my house. You can add of for clarity, but it’s not needed: haus (of) mi, haus (of) broder (of) mi = my brother’s house.
grammarOverview.bulletQuestions: Questions: Start with wat, hu, wer, wen, wai, hou.
